en: The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Practice Spoken by the Buddha, also titled the Sūtra on the Elder Vaiśya’s Inquiry into the Contemplation of Physical Conduct, translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of Henei during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Monastery, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

He was accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus as well as five thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were honored bodhisattvas—those whose supernatural powers were fully realized, who possessed the transformative power of skillful means and wisdom, and who traveled throughout the three thousandfold world system to universally benefit all beings, such that there was none who did not receive his salvation.

At that time, within the great city of Śrāvastī, there was a prominent elder named Virūḍhaka (translated into Chinese as Weishi). Together with five hundred other eminent elders of the city, who shared the same intention from previous lives, he departed from the great city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery.

They proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being before withdrawing to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, through his boundless penetration, questioned Vaiśya along with the elders and sons of noble families:
"What resolve have you set forth?"
"Shall we go to the Tathāgata?
At that time, Vaiśya and the elders immediately said to the Buddha,
"We shall, World-Honored One!"
Gathering together in a quiet place, they vied with one another in thought, saying:
"The appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter; likewise, obtaining a human body is rare. To be liberated from the world is equally very difficult."
We deliberated in private:
"By which vehicle shall we reach Nirvana?
Shall we attain Nirvana by means of the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas?"
"Are you liberated through the Mahāyāna’s universal wisdom and nirvāṇa?
At that time, we raised our minds and spoke these words:
"We vow for the unsurpassed vehicle; we shall not seek liberation through the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

"O World-Honored One! We have resolved our wills and generated the aspiration for the unsurpassed, peerless, and correct intention; it is for the sake of this Dharma that we have come to serve the Tathāgata.
How is this so, O World-Honored One?"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose inner nature constantly aspires to accord with unsurpassed, equal, true, and perfect awakening—what dharmas should they study, and how should they conduct themselves?
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to bestow his universal compassion through wisdom and, with boundless pity, dispel and reveal the knots of my doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vaiśya, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

These great elders are indeed able to reform their customs, renounce worldly glory and pleasure, and give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, true, and perfect enlightenment to come into the presence of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Viśeṣamati and the others, listen attentively and reflect upon this,
for I shall now expound the conduct of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, how they attain unexcelled, supreme, and perfect awakening, and the resolve and dharmas that correspond to their realization.
The householder Vaiśya and his five hundred followers all immediately joined their palms in reverence, received the instruction, and listened.
Then the Buddha addressed them, saying: "O householders!"

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sets forth on the path, desiring to correspond with unsurpassed, perfect, true, and equal supreme enlightenment, they should direct their mind toward sentient beings and establish vast, universal, and infinite great compassion. They should be resolved to practice mindfulness and conduct with diligent persistence, never abandoning it, and advance in learning without forgetfulness; this is how one corresponds to the path of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Furthermore, O householders!

If there are sentient beings who share in the evil deeds of body, speech, and mind they have committed, because they have practiced what is unwholesome, they will fall into hell at the end of their lives.
"O householders!

Heaven and earth converge, gathering manifold sufferings; toward all classes of sentient beings caught within the net of views, you should maintain a mind of great kindness and exert yourselves with great compassion;
thus should you preserve, practice, and study with such single-minded dedication."
His body was not clothed in garments nor sustained by food and drink, and his mind felt no greed for any gain or offerings; regarding all precious things, he delighted in giving them away entirely.
Mindful of those sentient beings, he carefully practiced and perfected the precepts, as well as patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom.
"In this way, householder!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to set forth upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path should practice the contemplation of dharmas and act accordingly with their body.
At that time, Vaiśya and the other householders:
“World-Honored One! We shall cultivate the three dharmas of mindfulness regarding the body, the four regarding speech, and the three regarding the mind.
How, World-Honored One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the dharmas concerning bodily conduct?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vaiśya and the others:
“In this way, householder!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body through forty-two matters.”
Having performed this contemplation, one becomes free from the fetters and entanglements of conceptualization.
The mind, body, and consciousness—along with their attachments to a self, greed for the body and life-span, and all turbid, chaotic non-virtues—should be completely eliminated.
At that time, Vaiśya and the other elders received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!
Contemplate that the body is filthy and fundamentally impure; contemplate that the body is a place of stench where putrefaction accumulates;
contemplate that the body is precarious and fragile, destined for destruction; contemplate that the body lacks strength and must eventually disintegrate and scatter;

contemplate that the body is like an illusion, a transformation of the great elements; contemplate that the body is a vessel of foul secretions leaking from its nine orifices; and contemplate that the body is ablaze with lustful desire.

He contemplates the body as a blazing fire; he contemplates the body as being consumed by the poisonous fire of anger and malice; he contemplates the body as being shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and dense delusion, where the poisons abound;
he contemplates the body as a net, bound by the fetters of affection and craving; he contemplates the body as a festering wound, entwined by manifold afflictions;

he contemplates the body as a source of suffering, subject to the four hundred and four diseases; he contemplates the body as a foul dwelling inhabited by various species of worms; he contemplates the body as being without...
One constantly contemplates that the body will inevitably return to dust; one contemplates that the body is dull and ignorant, failing to realize the nature of phenomena;

one contemplates that the body is precarious and base, destined soon to decay and fall apart; one contemplates that the body is destitute, always harboring much anxiety; one contemplates that the body is insubstantial, where old age brings the ultimate suffering;

one contemplates that the body has no reliance, being a mere facade of ornamentation and pure deception; and one contemplates that the body is difficult to satisfy, receiving and holding [sustenance] without ever knowing contentment.
Contemplate the body as a nest where one receives various forms and desires; contemplate the body as being deluded by greed and attachment to the five pleasures;

contemplate the body as being shrouded in darkness while the mind harbors joy; contemplate the body as having no fixed abode, with its various births and deaths; contemplate the body as consciousness and memory that cherishes all that is base;
contemplate the body as having no true friend, for even the most cherished nourishment leads to separation; contemplate the body as a feast of many foods, swallowed like a fox.
Contemplate the body as a struggle of wolves; contemplate the body’s mechanisms as revolving through countless transformations; contemplate the body as being filled with food and drink;
contemplate the body as foul-smelling and full of pus and blood, beyond the reach of sight; contemplate the body as subject to destruction and following the law of impermanence;

contemplate the body as an enemy, constantly harboring resentment and harm; contemplate the body as feverish affliction, always harboring sorrow and entanglement; contemplate the body as a mere collection.
One observes that calamities arise from being deluded by the five aggregates; one observes the body as an instrument of suffering and the intense pain of birth and death;
one observes the body as non-self, a mere accumulation of various conditions; one observes the body as having no life-force, where male and female meet and then disperse;

one observes the body as empty, its faculties receiving all sensory objects; one observes the body as lacking reality, comparable to a phantom; and one observes the body as false and deceptive, its manifestations like a dream.

To contemplate the body as false and delusive, like a mirage; to contemplate the body as deceptive, analogous to an echo or a reflection—this is called the forty-two matters of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of contemplating the body, O Elder.
Those who do not contemplate in this way may become attached to the body, whereby the mind, spirit, and consciousness arise and cease.

When a bodhisattva has contemplated in such a manner, all attachment to body and life, craving for a self, the stains of doubt and delusion, as well as various sensual pleasures and the notion of permanence, are entirely eliminated.
Adhering to their resolve and maintaining single-mindedness, they do not begrudge their years or their lives; in this way, they swiftly fulfill the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

Such are called the elder bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who, having perfected the six virtues, employ skillful means to spread the teaching and quickly attain the unsurpassed, most perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Thereupon, the World-Honored One further elaborated upon the Dharma of bodily conduct, pronouncing these verses of praise:
"Extremely difficult is it to obtain birth as a human; Do not, therefore, commit evil deeds with the body.
Inevitably one will die and be cast into a tomb, To be devoured by foxes and wolves, or else to rot away."
Deceit and falsehood constantly delude my foolishness; I single-mindedly give rise to thoughts of greed and lust.
This body seeks nothing but to return again and again, suffering all manner of pains day and night.

Because of manifold sufferings, affliction is produced; the body is a festering boil filled with impurities, constantly oppressed by the extremes of hunger and thirst—how could a wise person ever crave such a life?

Constantly receiving bodies, one never grows weary; forcibly nurturing them as if they were dear kin, one commits many transgressions for the sake of seeing forms, and by that cause, undergoes the agonies of hell.
The body cannot be like a vajra; do not commit evil deeds because of it.
Though it may endure for a long time, it will ultimately return to death; therefore, arouse faith and recite the Buddha’s name at all times.
Though one nourishes the body for a long time with sweet delicacies and fragrant flowers, hunger and thirst will inevitably arise;
since they are not constant, what benefit is there even in such diligent effort?
If, through the accumulation of merit over kalpas, one again encounters the era of a Buddha, the Honored One among Men, one should constantly give rise to faith and refrain from committing offenses;
otherwise, one may fall into the three realms of suffering and its bitter poisons.
Even those with a maximum lifespan of ten billion years must strive with diligence as if extinguishing a fire;
how much more so for those with a hundred-year life who, through arrogance and indulgence, create the calamities of hell.
If one harbors thoughts of "self" and "mine," it is extremely difficult to obtain a human body;
constantly indulging the mind in the five pleasures, one merely amuses oneself—how could one know what lies beyond?
This pleasure shall not endure forever; the various poisons of suffering will arrive before long.
One should swiftly abandon all stinginess and greed, so that one may attain great and corresponding blessings.
Wealth and non-wealth are like a dream; one forcibly imposes these upon sentient beings, yet at any moment they may exist or suddenly vanish. Therefore, the wise do not begrudge their wealth.

If form is like an illusion or a magical transformation, appearing as false flowers of brilliant color—then who is deceiving whose body regarding these desires and wealth? The ignorant and turbid fall into perversion.
One brings about wealth and merit through manifold sufferings; by means of the body, one employs mindfulness and perception.
Since wealth and non-wealth are matters of the five aggregates, what wise person would be deluded by such riches?
Falsely complying with wife and children, one’s amassed wealth is forcibly seized by royal power;
realizing impermanence is thus, one ultimately has no desire for the benefit of the household.
The gathering of affection and love brings forth suffering; do not be deluded by attachment to the prison of the household.
Parents, wealth, body, and wife and children—all must be left behind when one departs for the next life.
There are those who are greedy and possessive, unaware of their own state, fearing only that their wealth will perish along with them;
the foolish and stubborn strive diligently for riches, while the wise and discerning place their trust in non-attachment.

One who is stingy and lacks faith is not to be followed; though as humble as a child or a servant, they are externally parched with greed and internally feverish with flattery—such a person is not praised by the noble sages.
Speaking of books or poetic verses to delude the masses like a courtesan,
with a coarse mind and a violent, wicked nature— such are the many stingy people full of envy and jealousy.
The greedy and lustful nature has no true friends; though it displays humility to force intimacy with others, it pursues suffering solely for the sake of wealth.
Those possessed of wisdom and discernment should not trust it.
Because of following after wealth, one gives rise to this matter and conceives a mind of malice;
therefore, the wise should examine themselves and abandon stinginess, envy, and all that is perverse.
Gold, jewels, and all manner of rare treasures are obtained through the blessings of merit;
for this reason, disputes arise, and thus this intention is regulated by means of the Dharma.
At that time, one may encounter the Honored One among Heroes, the Tathāgata Maitreya Buddha;
there shall indeed be a ground of golden jewels, so how could one know where else it might be?
The five desires for pleasure are purely deceptive; the deluded mind is enticed by fraud.
Desire is like the intense heat of summer, causing exhaustion from chasing a mirage.
Greed for the desires of the eyes deludes oneself; lust arises, intoxicating and causing the loss of one's will.
Following habitual desire and succumbing to perversion—when shall we encounter the world of a Buddha?
Within ninety-one kalpas, a Buddha, the World-Honored One of Supreme Enlightenment, appears;
yet when Mount Sumeru is consumed and destroyed by fire, by what cause could one encounter him again in the future?
When the oceans, ponds, and pools have dried up, and heaven and earth are scorched until nothing remains, the blazing of desire is just like this; what wise person would be attached to desire?
All wise sages of penetrating intelligence should examine and know that they dwell in tranquility;
what craving could there be, and what is there to enjoy?
Understanding this meaning, one does not enter the net.
Meditative practice is the supreme method for training in the Dharma; do not cling to the prison of the cemetery.
If one harbors thoughts of attachment, affection, greed, and impurity, one cannot escape the calamities and suffering of the hells.
Though one has a wife and children, there is the suffering of separation; whatever deeds one performs, one must experience their results oneself.
Thus, one proceeds alone toward bitter suffering, for there is no one who can take one's pain.
Within these three realms, there is nothing that causes such intense affliction as wife and children;
though originally cherished for their provision and pleasure, they instead become the root of sorrow, transgression, and distress.
Because of clinging to sensation, one undergoes the suffering of the three evil realms; bitter, acrid, and agonizing pain arises.
If one were to be afflicted by the roots of affliction, even wife and children could not prevent it.

Do not think that because your father committed evil deeds, or your mother and various relatives did so, you will be spared from the agonies of Avīci hell; do not act as if your own conduct were irrelevant.

In the realm of King Yama and his hell-wardens, one is not questioned regarding the affairs of parents, nor brothers, wives, children, or friends; there, one’s own body alone is bound by its good and evil deeds.
Having attained this human body, one encounters and values the thought of not committing evil;
one cuts off and extinguishes all calamities and transgressions, and reforms former unwholesome deeds.
Having become turbid and defiled, guard yourself against concealment; do not believe that actions bear no retribution.
That Dharma King shall explain it in detail, distinguishing and clarifying how conduct becomes pure.
One must personally experience the consequences of the actions one has sown; if one lets the mind run wild, it will follow one into suffering.
Whatever the body creates, one immediately reaps the calamity, just as a shadow follows its form.
When one undergoes suffering and pain, neither parents nor kin can exempt one from it;
even those who are virtuous and close cannot substitute for one. Therefore, the wise have no attachment to desire.
Those who wish to escape the prison of suffering and torment, As well as the various bonds, shackles, and fetters,
Should diligently practice mindfulness and renounce desire, Swiftly following the Dharma taught by the Hero of the World.
The household is greatly ablaze, the root of much affliction; the fire has arisen and burns constantly.
What wise person would reach for and delight in this?
One must wipe away the great fire, fearing the midst of such hardship.
When householders grieve over profit, dwelling in worldly affairs to support their wives and children, they have these myriad anxieties;
why, then, would wisdom not lead one to renounce the home?
The teaching of the Ten Powers is most delightful; it is like obtaining roots where no seeds were planted.
Foolish children lack this resolve; they are merely deluded by their homes and fall into hell.
Those who are singularly deluded within heaven and earth give rise to thoughts of "my wife" and "my children";
with their foolish and stubborn minds they believe these exist permanently, unaware that they are but illusory manifestations.

When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had spoken this Dharma, the five hundred elders, including Vaiśravaṇa and the others, immediately attained the patient acceptance of the Dharma that accords with reality (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*).

Having attained this patience, they became fully endowed with supernormal powers; they mastered knowledge of the past and future, possessed vast and sublime noble wisdom, and their insight was unimpeded. They clearly understood the inclinations and desires of the minds of all sentient beings, for they had inspired all those gathered in the assembly to contemplate the nature of the mind.
He then spoke in verse:
"How wonderful! This is a great benefit, The most supreme among all benefits, For those who resolve their minds to practice And seek to become Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
The Mahāyāna mind is delightful; it seeks only to bring peace to sentient beings.
For the sake of others, they build bridges—those whose will delights in the Mahāyāna.
Sentient beings love and cherish them; all rejoice at the sight of their countenances.
Those who give rise to the awakened mind, Aiming to seek the bodhisattva path;
All who have generated the bodhicitta, Planting merit within the field of blessings;
And those who deeply delight in the bodhisattvas— They shall become luminaries for the triple world.
The mind of the Bodhisattva Loṅshèng (Exalted Saint) surpasses that of all the multitudes;
fully endowed with everything, he is able to deliver all sentient beings.
We have gained a most excellent benefit, for we joyfully give rise to this mind.
Having encountered the Buddha Śākyamuni, the Lion of Perfect Enlightenment,
and having attained the hearing of this Dharma, the Bodhisattva contemplates the nature of the body;
his resolve then delights in the Mahāyāna, and he attains the state of docility.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.

When the World-Honored One smiled, five-colored light issued forth from his mouth, radiant and brilliant, with each color distinct. It eventually reached countless lands throughout the ten directions, its majestic splendor eclipsing the brilliance of all the palaces of Śakra, Brahmā, the sun and moon, and the heavenly Māras.

When the Buddha smiled and emitted his covering light, seventy-two thousand devas, nāgas, spirits, and worldly people beheld the magnificent transformation of the Buddha’s divine radiance. They all realized for themselves that they were being illuminated and nurtured in their bodies by the Tathāgata’s brilliance; each, while still upon their seats, suddenly attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Furthermore, countless others all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Then, the flames circled his body three times, and his majestic light suddenly entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world, they bring peace and deliverance to sentient beings; as their teachings flow forth abundantly, they never smile without cause."
For what reason has Your Majesty now manifested such a majestic countenance and smiled with joy?
How excellent, World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has bestowed his virtue and compassionately regards all the immeasurable devas and the people of the world, enabling them all to attain peace. Even the beasts, birds, and all crawling and flying insects have not failed to receive his deliverance. We pray that the Buddha will explain and expound upon the meaning of this smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Do you see these five hundred people, including the householder Viśākha?
"Indeed, I see them," he replied.
The World-Honored One said:
"These elders have planted the roots of all virtues under past Buddhas, ever since they first resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment."
Thus it is, Ānanda!

After seventy-six kalpas have passed, the householder Vaiśya and his five hundred followers shall not fall into the three sufferings; thereafter, they shall attain Buddhahood within the same single kalpa. That kalpa shall be named *Vīrya* (Valiant), all sharing the same character. Their titles shall be Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat, each named Flower-Virtue-Treasury King (*Puṣpavicitra-garbharāja*). Each of them shall deliver beings to the utmost limit of the immeasurable.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
How profoundly subtle and marvelous this is; it is truly unprecedented.”
The Tathāgata has thus expounded this vast, profound, and boundless essential Dharma; what is the name of this sutra, and how should it be upheld?
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! This sūtra is titled ‘The Bodhisattva’s Practice,’ and it is also titled ‘The Sūtra on the Contemplation of Physical Conduct as Asked by Mahāsattva Vīryadatta.’”
Furthermore, Ānanda!

This essential method of contemplation is that by which all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have attained the Way and carried out their great transformation; there is no way they did not do so through it.

Now that I have attained Buddhahood and possess the physical marks and signs of excellence, I transform beings within the cycle of birth and death by means of this very Dharma; you should therefore skillfully copy, uphold, recite, read, explain, and reveal it to all.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the Great Being Viśeṣacinti, the five hundred men and their peers, as well as the devas, nāgas, spirits, and the people of the world, rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; they all rose with palms joined and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Bodhisattva’s Cultivation of Practice
